lead: A VLSI design flow is the ordered set of stages that turns a written specification into a tested silicon chip. It exists because a chip with millions of gates cannot be designed in one jump; each stage solves a smaller, checkable problem. The flow splits into front-end work (specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis) and back-end work (DFT insertion, floorplan, placement, clock tree, routing, signoff, tapeout, package, test). Fabless companies, foundries and service firms all follow roughly this order for phone SoCs, set-top boxes and payment-terminal chips.
prereq: You need: basic digital logic — gates, flip-flops, Boolean algebra, binary numbers; the rest of this unit builds on it, starting with 5.2 Verilog HDL.

blocks.text: A flow is an order of stages. Each stage takes one description of the chip and produces a more concrete one. Early stages stay in text and netlists; late stages deal with rectangles on the die.

items: Specification: function, clock frequency in MHz or GHz, power in W, cost, package, interfaces.
Architecture: partition into blocks, count clock domains, fix bus widths, memory sizes and I/O pins.
RTL: write the design as register-transfer-level Verilog modules (5.2, 5.3).
Verification: simulate against a test bench and add formal proofs (5.4).
Synthesis: map RTL to a gate netlist of standard cells under a clock-period constraint.
DFT insertion: add scan chains and self-test logic while the design is still a netlist.
Physical design: floorplan, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing (5.6).
Signoff: design-rule check (DRC), layout-versus-schematic (LVS), timing, power, IR drop.
Tapeout: release masks, fabricate, package, test on the tester.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call everything up to the gate netlist the front-end flow and everything from DFT insertion to tapeout the back-end flow. The order is top-down: the specification is refined into blocks, blocks into RTL, RTL into gates. Real projects also work bottom-up, reusing verified blocks so a stage is never started from zero. Verification is not one stage — it runs beside RTL and continues to signoff.

items: Full-custom: every transistor is drawn by hand. Best speed, power and area, highest design cost. Used for SRAM cells, PLLs and high-speed datapaths.
Semi-custom: pre-designed standard cells in rows, placed and routed automatically. Most digital logic is built this way.
ASIC: an application-specific integrated circuit — a chip designed for one product, usually semi-custom.
SoC: a system on chip — processor, memories, peripherals and analog on one die, assembled mostly from IP blocks (5.7).

blocks.text: At block level the flow fixes the boring but fatal details: the clock plan (PLL, clock domains, reset distribution), the I/O ring (pads, electrostatic discharge protection, level shifters), the device modes (functional, scan, self-test, sleep), the memories (compiled SRAM macros with fixed shapes), the analog blocks (PLL, ADC, voltage regulator) and power management (voltage islands, power gating, isolation cells, retention flip-flops). A wrong clock or reset decision found at signoff costs weeks; found in the specification it costs an hour.

A finished chip must be testable on a tester costing crores, so the design team hands the test team three things: the DUT (design under test, the netlist), the inserted DFT hardware, and the pattern set. The pattern set comes from ATPG (automatic test pattern generation), which works from the netlist plus a fault model; fault simulation grades how many modelled faults the patterns detect, reported as coverage in percent. BIST puts a pattern generator and checker on the chip itself, common for memories.

head: Fault model
What it models
rows: A line too slow to rise or fall
A short that appears only on switching
A tiny extra delay below TDF resolution

blocks.text: Test cost in rupees is roughly tester time per pattern × number of patterns × tester rate, so coverage is traded against tester hours. Unit 6 covers the fault models, ATPG algorithms, scan design and BIST in detail.

examples.question: An SoC has 2.4 million standard-cell gates. Synthesis runs at 120k gates per hour, placement and routing together run at 60k gates per hour, and verification needs 3 hours per 10 000 gates. Find the synthesis time, the physical-design time, the verification time, the total flow time, and the verification share of that total.
steps: Total time = 20 h + 40 h + 720 h = 780 h.
examples.answer: Synthesis 20 h, physical design 40 h, verification 720 h, total 780 h, and verification is 92.3% of the flow.
examples.check:
gates = 2_400_000
syn_rate = 120_000
pdr_rate = 60_000
ver_hours_per_10k = 3.0
syn_h = gates / syn_rate
pdr_h = gates / pdr_rate
blocks = gates / 10_000
ver_h = blocks * ver_hours_per_10k
total_h = syn_h + pdr_h + ver_h
share = ver_h / total_h * 100
print(int(syn_h))
print(int(pdr_h))
print(int(ver_h))
print(int(total_h))
print(round(share, 1))

traps: Do not draw the flow as one straight line. Verification runs beside every stage and DFT insertion happens before physical design, so a spec → RTL → synthesis → layout → tapeout answer loses marks.
The front-end flow ends at the gate netlist (synthesis), not at RTL; floorplan and routing are back-end.
DFT is not testing. DFT adds on-chip hardware during design; the tester applies ATPG patterns after fabrication.
High stuck-at coverage does not mean zero escapes — transition and path delay defects, bridging and Iddq need their own models.
DFT must be inserted before physical design, because scan chains have to be placed, buffered and timed like any other logic.

quiz.q: Define the front-end and back-end parts of the VLSI design flow.
quiz.a: Front-end: specification, architecture, RTL, verification, synthesis, ending at the gate netlist. Back-end: DFT insertion, floorplan, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing, signoff and tapeout.

quiz.q: What does ATPG produce, and what does fault simulation do with it?
quiz.a: ATPG produces test patterns from the netlist and a fault model; fault simulation reports the fraction of modelled faults those patterns detect, as coverage in percent.

quiz.q: Why does verification run beside RTL instead of waiting for the gate netlist?
quiz.a: A bug found in RTL costs an edit and a re-run; the same bug found after synthesis or routing forces re-synthesis or re-layout, and after tapeout it forces a new mask set. Early checking is orders of magnitude cheaper.

quiz.q: Give one reason DFT insertion is placed before physical design.
quiz.a: The added scan chains and self-test logic must be placed, buffered and timed with the rest of the logic. Inserting them after routing would change the netlist and break timing and design rules.

quiz.q: A block has 1.5 million gates and synthesis runs at 150k gates per hour. How long does synthesis take?
A team tapes out at 99.8% stuck-at coverage. One chip fails at full clock speed in the lab. Which fault models were probably not covered, and why?
quiz.a: Stuck-at patterns catch lines fixed at 0 or 1, usually applied slowly. A part that works slowly but fails at speed points to transition delay, path delay or small delay defects, and possibly resistive bridging; these need at-speed transition and path patterns.

quiz.q: In the worked example verification takes 720 h of 780 h. Give one reason this share grows with gate count and one way to cut it.
quiz.a: Verification effort grows with the number of states and corner cases and is hard to parallelise cheaply, while synthesis and place-and-route scale better with tool capacity. Ways to cut it: reuse already-verified IP, drive simulation by coverage instead of random runs, and use formal proofs on small blocks.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the flow now runs on cloud farms where a single synthesis job is split across hundreds of machines. Open-source flows built from Yosys for synthesis and OpenROAD for placement and routing, with public process design kits, let students tape out small chips. Chiplets and 2.5D packaging are shifting the flow from one big die to several verified dies joined by short links, which moves test to the package boundary. Machine learning is used for placement, clock-tree tuning and test-pattern selection. Search next: logic synthesis constraints (SDC), UPF power intent, chiplet test, and design-technology co-optimisation.
